Exercise 3.1b — One workflow, two models

In R, you can fit a linear regression directly with lm(). In this practical you will use lm() as the engine inside the familiar tidymodels steps: specify a model, fit it on training patients, and call predict() for held-out patients. In Python the same three steps are LinearRegression(), .fit() and .predict() from scikit-learn.

  • Part 1. Predict blood glucose from age. Calculate the prediction for a 45-year-old by hand from the fitted equation, check it with predict(), and see the point on the fitted line. Compare predictions with the measured glucose of the test patients, then refit with different training patients to see how the line and the predictions change.
  • Part 2. Add BMI, repeat the hand calculation, and find the prediction on the fitted plane in a 3D plot you can turn.
  • Part 3. Keep the same steps, training patients and predictors, and fit a decision tree instead. Follow the same patient through the splits, read the prediction from the leaf, check it with predict(), and compare the tree’s stepped surface with the regression plane.
NoteThe plots are for looking at

The code for the plots is folded away under Code for this plot (optional). You do not need to write it, but it is in the download if you want it.

  • R
  • Python

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot", "plotly"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)

theme_set(theme_bw())

data/glucose_bmi_study.csv holds the same 80 patients as data/glucose_study.csv, with one more column: BMI in kg/m². If you do not have it yet, download glucose_bmi_study.csv into your data folder.

glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_bmi_study.csv")

summary(glu)
#>       age             BMI           glucose      
#>  Min.   :21.00   Min.   : 0.00   Min.   : 72.00  
#>  1st Qu.:23.00   1st Qu.:27.60   1st Qu.: 99.75  
#>  Median :28.00   Median :31.80   Median :115.00  
#>  Mean   :33.26   Mean   :31.53   Mean   :119.90  
#>  3rd Qu.:42.00   3rd Qu.:37.45   3rd Qu.:129.75  
#>  Max.   :81.00   Max.   :57.30   Max.   :199.00

Three patients have a BMI of 0, which is impossible: a missing value recorded as 0, as you saw on Day 2. Remove them.

glu <- glu |>
  filter(BMI > 0)

nrow(glu)
#> [1] 77

Split the 77 patients into training and test patients, as on Day 1.

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8)

train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

cat(nrow(train), "training patients,", nrow(test), "test patients\n")
#> 61 training patients, 16 test patients

Part 1 — Predict glucose from age

The same three steps as on Day 1: specify the model, fit it on the training patients, predict.

# 1. Specify: linear regression, computed by lm()
lm_model <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

# 2. Fit on the training patients
line_fit <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = train)

# the learned parameters: intercept first, then the slope
b <- line_fit$fit$coefficients
b
#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 111.7974710   0.2495637

The fitted equation is

\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age}\]

Task 1a — A 45-year-old, by hand

Read the two parameters printed above, round them to two decimals, and calculate the predicted glucose for a 45-year-old.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_45 <- ______ + ______ * 45
predicted_45
TipStuck?

The first number is the intercept, \(\hat\beta_0\). The second is the slope, \(\hat\beta_1\), which multiplies the age.

Now check it with predict(), which uses the unrounded parameters:

# predict() wants a data frame: one row, one column per predictor
predict(line_fit, new_data = tibble(age = 45))$.pred
#> [1] 123.0278

The two agree to within a few hundredths: the difference is only the rounding.

Code for this plot (optional) 
ggplot(train, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = b[1], slope = b[2],
              colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = 45, y = predict(line_fit, new_data = tibble(age = 45))$.pred,
           colour = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "Training patients, the fitted line, and the 45-year-old")

Task 1b — Predictions against measured glucose

The test patients were not used to fit the line. Predict their glucose and put it next to what was measured.

test_results <- test |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(line_fit, new_data = test)$.pred,
         gap = glucose - predicted)

test_results

Code for this plot (optional) 
ggplot(test_results, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = b[1], slope = b[2],
              colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = age, y = glucose, yend = predicted),
               colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(y = glucose), colour = "darkorange", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "Test patients: measured (orange) and predicted (on the line)")
ImportantThink about it
  1. How far are the predictions from the measured glucose, typically?
  2. All 16 predictions lie in a narrow band. Why?

Task 1c — Different training patients

Split again with a different seed, refit, and compare.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
split_1 <- initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8)
train_1 <- training(split_1)

line_fit_1 <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = ______)

line_fit_1$fit$coefficients
predict(line_fit_1, new_data = tibble(age = ______))$.pred
TipStuck?

Nothing about the model changes: lm_model is the same specification. Only the training patients change, and the patient you predict for is the same 45-year-old.

Twenty different splits, twenty different lines:

Code for this plot (optional) 
lines_20 <- tibble()
for (s in 1:20) {
  set.seed(s)
  train_s <- training(initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8))
  fit_s <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = train_s)
  lines_20 <- bind_rows(lines_20, tibble(
    seed = s,
    intercept = fit_s$fit$coefficients[1],
    slope = fit_s$fit$coefficients[2]))
}

ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_abline(data = lines_20, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope),
              colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "The fitted line from 20 different training splits")
ImportantThink about it

Where do the 20 lines agree most, and where do they spread out? What does that mean for a prediction at age 25 compared with age 75?

Part 2 — Add BMI

The same specification, lm_model, with a second predictor:

plane_fit <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age + BMI, data = train)

plane_fit$fit$coefficients
#> (Intercept)         age         BMI 
#>  77.7019532   0.1982922   1.1144423

\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \times \text{BMI}\]

With two predictors the model is no longer a line but a flat plane above the age–BMI floor.

Task 2a — The same patient, now with a BMI of 30

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_patient <- ______ + ______ * 45 + ______ * 30
predicted_patient
TipStuck?

Three parameters, in the order printed: the intercept, the weight for age, the weight for BMI.

Check it with predict():

patient <- tibble(age = 45, BMI = 30)

predict(plane_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred
#> [1] 120.0584

Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom. The red point is the patient, sitting on the plane.

Code for this plot (optional) 
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
# every combination of age and BMI on a fine grid
grid <- expand_grid(age = seq(20, 82, by = 0.5),
                    BMI = seq(19, 47, by = 0.5))
ages <- unique(grid$age)
bmis <- unique(grid$BMI)

# the plane's prediction at each grid point, as a matrix:
# one row per BMI value, one column per age
plane_matrix <- matrix(predict(plane_fit, new_data = grid)$.pred,
                       nrow = length(bmis))

fig_plane <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_markers(data = train, x = ~age, y = ~BMI, z = ~glucose,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                      name = "Training patients") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = plane_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.6, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("lightgrey", "grey")),
                      name = "Plane") |>
  plotly::add_markers(x = 45, y = 30,
                      z = predict(plane_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred,
                      marker = list(size = 7, color = "red"),
                      name = "Age 45, BMI 30") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Glucose (mg/dL)")))
fig_plane
ImportantThink about it
  1. In words, what does the BMI weight mean?
  2. Adding BMI moved this patient’s prediction by how much? Does a second predictor guarantee better predictions?

Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree

Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the fit() and predict() calls stay the same.

# 1. Specify: a regression tree, computed by rpart
tree_model <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_fit <- tree_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age + BMI, data = train)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, type = 3, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = "Blues", roundint = FALSE)

Each box asks a yes/no question. Yes goes left, no goes right. The number in each leaf at the bottom is the prediction: the mean glucose of the training patients who ended up there.

Task 3a — Follow the patient

Start at the top with the patient aged 45 with a BMI of 30. At each question, go left or right. Which leaf do you reach, and what glucose does it predict?

Check it with predict():

predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred
#> [1] 129.2941

Turn the plot. The orange surface is the tree, the grey one the plane from Part 2.

Code for this plot (optional) 
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
# the tree's prediction on the same grid as the plane
tree_matrix <- matrix(predict(tree_fit, new_data = grid)$.pred,
                      nrow = length(bmis))

fig_tree <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_markers(data = train, x = ~age, y = ~BMI, z = ~glucose,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                      name = "Training patients") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = tree_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.8, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("moccasin", "darkorange")),
                      name = "Tree") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = plane_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.5, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("lightgrey", "grey")),
                      name = "Plane") |>
  plotly::add_markers(x = 45, y = 30,
                      z = predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred,
                      marker = list(size = 7, color = "red"),
                      name = "Age 45, BMI 30 (tree)") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Glucose (mg/dL)")))
fig_tree
ImportantThink about it
  1. Describe the shape of the tree’s surface. Why is it made of flat steps?
  2. This tree never asks about BMI. What does that do to its surface, and why might it have ignored BMI?
  3. A new patient is 90 years old, older than anyone in the training data. What do the plane and the tree predict, and why do they behave differently?
ImportantLearning points
  • The steps are the same whatever the model: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. Swapping linear regression for a tree changed one line.
  • A linear model’s prediction can be worked out by hand from its parameters; a tree’s prediction is read by following the questions to a leaf.
  • The fitted model depends on which patients were used for training.
  • A line or plane changes smoothly and keeps going beyond the data; a tree predicts in flat steps and stays within the values it saw.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn plotly

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, plot_tree, export_text

data/glucose_bmi_study.csv holds the same 80 patients as data/glucose_study.csv, with one more column: BMI in kg/m². If you do not have it yet, download glucose_bmi_study.csv into your data folder.

glu = pd.read_csv("data/glucose_bmi_study.csv")

glu.describe()
#>              age        BMI     glucose
#> count  80.000000  80.000000   80.000000
#> mean   33.262500  31.533750  119.900000
#> std    13.798499   9.436409   29.565461
#> min    21.000000   0.000000   72.000000
#> 25%    23.000000  27.600000   99.750000
#> 50%    28.000000  31.800000  115.000000
#> 75%    42.000000  37.450000  129.750000
#> max    81.000000  57.300000  199.000000

Three patients have a BMI of 0, which is impossible: a missing value recorded as 0, as you saw on Day 2. Remove them.

glu = glu[glu["BMI"] > 0]

len(glu)
#> 77

Split the 77 patients into training and test patients, as on Day 1.

train, test = train_test_split(glu, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

print(len(train), "training patients,", len(test), "test patients")
#> 61 training patients, 16 test patients
NoteThe numbers differ from the R tab

Python and R shuffle with different random number generators, so random_state=42 and set.seed(42) do not choose the same training patients. Expect different numbers from the R tab; the steps are the same.

Part 1 — Predict glucose from age

The same three steps as on Day 1: specify the model, fit it on the training patients, predict.

# 1. Specify: linear regression
line_model = LinearRegression()

# 2. Fit on the training patients: predictors (a table) and outcome
line_model.fit(train[["age"]], train["glucose"])
LinearRegression()
In a Jupyter environment, please rerun this cell to show the HTML representation or trust the notebook.
On GitHub, the HTML representation is unable to render, please try loading this page with nbviewer.org.
Parameters
fit_intercept fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set
to False, no intercept will be used in calculations
(i.e. data is expected to be centered).		 True
copy_X copy_X: bool, default=True

If True, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.		 True
tol tol: float, default=1e-6

The precision of the solution (`coef_`) is determined by `tol` which
specifies the convergence criterion of the underlying solver. `tol` is
set as `atol` and `btol` of :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr` when
fitting on sparse training data. `tol` is set as `cond` of
:func:`scipy.linalg.lstsq` when fitting on dense training data.

.. versionadded:: 1.7
.. versionchanged:: 1.9
Now supported on dense data, interpreted as the `cond` parameter.		 1e-06
n_jobs n_jobs: int, default=None

The number of jobs to use for the computation. This will only provide
speedup in case of sufficiently large problems, that is if firstly
`n_targets > 1` and secondly `X` is sparse or if `positive` is set
to `True`. ``None`` means 1 unless in a
:obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context. ``-1`` means using all
processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>` for more details.		 None
positive positive: bool, default=False

When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive. This
option is only supported for dense arrays.

For a comparison between a linear regression model with positive constraints
on the regression coefficients and a linear regression without such constraints,
see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_nnls.py`.

# the learned parameters
print("intercept:", line_model.intercept_)
#> intercept: 100.82493771255302
print("slope:", line_model.coef_)
#> slope: [0.48966996]

The fitted equation is

\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age}\]

Task 1a — A 45-year-old, by hand

Read the two parameters printed above, round them to two decimals, and calculate the predicted glucose for a 45-year-old.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_45 = ______ + ______ * 45
predicted_45
TipStuck?

The intercept is \(\hat\beta_0\). The slope, \(\hat\beta_1\), multiplies the age.

Now check it with predict(), which uses the unrounded parameters:

# predict() wants a table: one row, one column per predictor
line_model.predict(pd.DataFrame({"age": [45]}))
#> array([122.86008596])

The two agree to within about a tenth: the difference is only the rounding.

Code for this plot (optional) 
ages_line = np.array([20, 82])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(train["age"], train["glucose"], color="steelblue")
ax.plot(ages_line, line_model.intercept_ + line_model.coef_[0] * ages_line,
        "r--", linewidth=1)
ax.scatter([45], line_model.predict(pd.DataFrame({"age": [45]})),
           color="red", s=60, zorder=3)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_title("Training patients, the fitted line, and the 45-year-old")
plt.show()

Task 1c — Different training patients

Split again with a different seed, refit, and compare.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
train_1, test_1 = train_test_split(glu, test_size=0.2, random_state=1)

line_model_1 = LinearRegression()
line_model_1.fit(______[["age"]], ______["glucose"])

TipStuck?

Nothing about the model changes. Only the training patients change, and the patient you predict for is the same 45-year-old.

Twenty different splits, twenty different lines:

Code for this plot (optional) 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], color="grey")

    model_s = LinearRegression().fit(train_s[["age"]], train_s["glucose"])
    ax.plot(ages_line, model_s.intercept_ + model_s.coef_[0] * ages_line,

Part 2 — Add BMI

The same kind of model, with a second predictor:

plane_model = LinearRegression()
plane_model.fit(train[["age", "BMI"]], train["glucose"])
#> LinearRegression()
print("intercept:", plane_model.intercept_)
#> intercept: 82.06015127140364
print("weights (age, BMI):", plane_model.coef_)
#> weights (age, BMI): [0.45862511 0.61087004]

\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \times \text{BMI}\]

With two predictors the model is no longer a line but a flat plane above the age–BMI floor.

Task 2a — The same patient, now with a BMI of 30

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_patient = ______ + ______ * 45 + ______ * 30
predicted_patient
TipStuck?

Three parameters: the intercept, then the two weights in the order of the columns, age first and BMI second.

Check it with predict():

patient = pd.DataFrame({"age": [45], "BMI": [30]})

plane_model.predict(patient)
#> array([121.02438232])

Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom. The red point is the patient, sitting on the plane.

Code for this plot (optional) 
# This plot needs the plotly package: pip install plotly
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# every combination of age and BMI on a fine grid
ages = np.arange(20, 82.5, 0.5)
bmis = np.arange(19, 47.5, 0.5)
A, B = np.meshgrid(ages, bmis)
grid = pd.DataFrame({"age": A.ravel(), "BMI": B.ravel()})

# the plane's prediction at each grid point: one row per BMI, one column per age
plane_matrix = plane_model.predict(grid).reshape(A.shape)

fig_plane = go.Figure()
fig_plane.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(
    x=train["age"], y=train["BMI"], z=train["glucose"], mode="markers",
    marker={"size": 3, "color": "steelblue"}, name="Training patients"))
fig_plane.add_trace(go.Surface(
    x=ages, y=bmis, z=plane_matrix, opacity=0.6, showscale=False,
    colorscale=[[0, "lightgrey"], [1, "grey"]], name="Plane"))
fig_plane.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(
    x=[45], y=[30], z=plane_model.predict(patient), mode="markers",
    marker={"size": 7, "color": "red"}, name="Age 45, BMI 30"))
fig_plane.update_layout(scene={"xaxis_title": "Age (years)",
                               "yaxis_title": "BMI (kg/m²)",
                               "zaxis_title": "Glucose (mg/dL)"})
fig_plane.show()
ImportantThink about it
  1. In words, what does the BMI weight mean?
  2. Adding BMI moved this patient’s prediction by how much? Does a second predictor guarantee better predictions?

Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree

Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the .fit() and .predict() calls stay the same.

# 1. Specify: a regression tree, kept small enough to follow by hand
tree_model = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=7,
                                   random_state=0)

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_model.fit(train[["age", "BMI"]], train["glucose"])
#> DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=7, random_state=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
plot_tree(tree_model, feature_names=["age", "BMI"], filled=True,
          impurity=False, precision=1, ax=ax)
#> [Text(0.5, 0.875, 'age <= 23.5\nsamples = 61\nvalue = 117.4'), Text(0.25, 0.625, 'BMI <= 27.7\nsamples = 14\nvalue = 94.3'), Text(0.375, 0.75, 'True  '), Text(0.125, 0.375, 'samples = 7\nvalue = 91.6'), Text(0.375, 0.375, 'samples = 7\nvalue = 97.0'), Text(0.75, 0.625, 'BMI <= 41.0\nsamples = 47\nvalue = 124.3'), Text(0.625, 0.75, '  False'), Text(0.625, 0.375, 'age <= 26.5\nsamples = 40\nvalue = 126.8'), Text(0.5, 0.125, 'samples = 11\nvalue = 116.4'), Text(0.75, 0.125, 'samples = 29\nvalue = 130.8'), Text(0.875, 0.375, 'samples = 7\nvalue = 109.7')]
plt.show()

Each box asks a yes/no question. True goes left, False goes right. The value in each leaf at the bottom is the prediction: the mean glucose of the training patients who ended up there. max_depth=3 allows at most three questions in a row, and min_samples_leaf=7 requires at least seven training patients in every leaf; without them the tree would keep splitting until it was too large to follow.

Task 3a — Follow the patient

Start at the top with the patient aged 45 with a BMI of 30. At each question, go left or right. Which leaf do you reach, and what glucose does it predict?

Check it with predict():

tree_model.predict(patient)
#> array([130.79310345])

Turn the plot. The orange surface is the tree, the grey one the plane from Part 2.

Code for this plot (optional) 
# the tree's prediction on the same grid as the plane
tree_matrix = tree_model.predict(grid).reshape(A.shape)

fig_tree = go.Figure()
fig_tree.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(
    x=train["age"], y=train["BMI"], z=train["glucose"], mode="markers",
    marker={"size": 3, "color": "steelblue"}, name="Training patients"))
fig_tree.add_trace(go.Surface(
    x=ages, y=bmis, z=tree_matrix, opacity=0.8, showscale=False,
    colorscale=[[0, "moccasin"], [1, "darkorange"]], name="Tree"))
fig_tree.add_trace(go.Surface(
    x=ages, y=bmis, z=plane_matrix, opacity=0.5, showscale=False,
    colorscale=[[0, "lightgrey"], [1, "grey"]], name="Plane"))
fig_tree.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(
    x=[45], y=[30], z=tree_model.predict(patient), mode="markers",
    marker={"size": 7, "color": "red"}, name="Age 45, BMI 30 (tree)"))
fig_tree.update_layout(scene={"xaxis_title": "Age (years)",
                              "yaxis_title": "BMI (kg/m²)",
                              "zaxis_title": "Glucose (mg/dL)"})
fig_tree.show()
ImportantThink about it
  1. Describe the shape of the tree’s surface. Why is it made of flat steps?
  2. Which predictor does the tree ask about first, and how often does it ask about BMI? Compare with how much BMI changed the plane in Part 2.
  3. A new patient is 90 years old, older than anyone in the training data. What do the plane and the tree predict, and why do they behave differently?
ImportantLearning points
  • The steps are the same whatever the model: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. Swapping linear regression for a tree changed one line.
  • A linear model’s prediction can be worked out by hand from its parameters; a tree’s prediction is read by following the questions to a leaf.
  • The fitted model depends on which patients were used for training.
  • A line or plane changes smoothly and keeps going beyond the data; a tree predicts in flat steps and stays within the values it saw.
